tldr: Blanc live-codes a waffle-shop REST app on Vidocq, a zero-dependency Jakarta EE Core Profile and MicroProfile implementation built by coding agents from specs and TCKs, then secures it with an OIDC server built the same way.
summary: Sébastien Blanc (SCIAM) explains that Vidocq began at the JChateau unconference as an experiment by two colleagues. Since LLMs work well with detailed specs and Jakarta EE comes with specs plus TCKs, could an agent build a CDI implementation using only the JDK? It grew to about 300,000 lines and 19 components covering most of Core Profile and MicroProfile, all as proper JPMS modules with no third-party dependencies, which the team presents as a European sovereign stack. In dev mode with live reload, he builds a JAX-RS menu endpoint, injects a MicroProfile Config property, and tours the new dev console (REST endpoints, OpenAPI, health, config, logs, JVM state, and Postgres dev services in progress) and the vidocq CLI for adding extensions.

He then adds an order service and resource and secures them with @RolesAllowed("customer") and an injected SecurityContext that records who placed each order. As the identity provider he uses Rossignol, an OpenID Connect server he vibe-coded on top of Vidocq. It already supports realms, key management, users and the authorization code flow, though he says it is not production-ready. Unauthenticated calls return 401, and after logging in as Alice through a Python helper script the order succeeds. In the last minute he asks OpenCode, using a Vidocq skill, to generate a kitchen service, but time runs out before it finishes.
keyPoints: Vidocq was generated by coding agents guided by Jakarta EE/MicroProfile specs and validated against official TCKs; about 300k lines and 19 components so far.
It uses no external dependencies beyond the JDK and is fully modular (module-info, no automatic modules).
Developer experience includes Maven dev mode with live reload, a dev console (OpenAPI, health, config, logs) and a CLI for managing extensions.
Security works with standard @RolesAllowed and SecurityContext against Rossignol, an experimental OIDC provider also built on Vidocq.
The final vibe-coding step with OpenCode and a Vidocq skill did not complete within the time slot.
takeaways: Try Vidocq for a small JAX-RS/CDI/MicroProfile service if you want a dependency-free Jakarta stack.
If you experiment with agent-built software, give the agent formal specs and a test suite such as TCKs to validate against.
Treat Rossignol and snapshot builds as experimental; do not put them in production yet.

quotes.text: It goes even faster than JavaScript frameworks.

watchIf: You are curious whether coding agents plus specs and TCKs can produce a working Jakarta EE runtime, and want to see what building on it looks like today.
